full_judgment:
9. As per the earliest decision on the subject, in the case of Gobinda Chandra Saha v. Dwarka Nath Patita, (1) Mookerjee and Walmsley, JJ. held that an endorsement by a postal peon can at best be a record of a statement by the peon. Such statement will be admissible u/s. 32(2) of the Evidence Act: It could also be admissible u/s. 33 of the Evidence Act. The endorsement is not even admissible as statement made by a public officer in the discharge of his duty. Now would the endorsement attract the presumption contained in Section 114, illustration (f) of the Evidence Act. There is no presumption that the cover has been tendered to the addressee on a particular date. "The presumption mentioned is Section 114 is not a presumption of law but a presumption of fact, and where, as in this case, the defendant pledges his oath that the cover was never tendered to him, we cannot treat the presumption of regularity of official business as conclusive against him." 

 12. In the then Dacca High Court this question came up for consideration in the case of Monomohem Roy v. Ajit Kumar Duita (4). This was a case where the validity of a notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was involved. The notice was registered and it came back with a postal endorsement 'refused'. The peon was of course examined in this case by the plaintiff. Nevertheless it was held that it is on the defendant to prove that the letter was not properly addressed to him or it was never tendered to him. The plaintiff need not prove the service of registered letter duly addressed which has come back with an endorsement "refused". He can rely on the presumption under section 114 illustration (f) of the Evidence Act that a common course of business has been followed in a particular that there are that though it the presumption case Chowdhury, J. observed cases where it has been held is open to the Court to raise it cannot held that posting proves delivery. But his Lordship observes that preponderance of authority is on the other side. His Lordship notes the aforesited cases reported in 39 C.W.N. 934 and 52 C.W.N. 659. His Lordship also referred to the case of Harihar Banerjl v. Ramshashi Roy and ers. (5) where their Lordships of the Privy Council held that if a letter properly directed, containing a notice to quit, was proved to have been put into the post office, it was presumed that the letter reached its designation at the proper time according to the regular course of business of the post office, and was received by the person to whom it was addressed, and that presumption would apply with greater force to registered letter. 

 13. In the Calcutta High Court itself the decision reported in AIR 1915 Calcutta 313 was dissented from even in respect of a notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Sushil Kumar Chakravarty v. Ganesh Chandra Mitre, (6) a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court held that where a notice to quit, after being properly addressed, prepaid and posted by registered post, is returned with the endorsement "refused", two different presumptions are of assistance to the plaintiff. One is the presumption as mentioned in illustration (f) of Section 114 of the Evidence Act and the other is the presumption contained in illustration (e) of Section 114 of the Evidence Act. These two presumptions entitled the Court to hold, firstly, that the endorsement has been made actually by the peon and-than that the endorsement "refused" is a correct statement of fact. If there is evidence to the contrary and that evidence is believed by the court, the presumption must be held to the rebutted. An argument was advanced in this case that as soon as there was denial of the service by the defendant the presumption stood rebutted and the decision contained in AIR 1915 Cal 313 was cited to be the authority for this proposition. The Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court was unable to see anything in that case to support this submission. Apart from the presumption contained in illustrations (e) and (f) of Section 114 of the Evidence Act, the Division Bench also held that a notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act sent by registered post can also attract the presumption u/s. 27 of the General Clauses Act. 

 14. The same question cropped up in the case of Alauddin v. Md. Idris Mia (1) There also the validity of a notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was in question. A notice sent by registered post was returned with the endorsement "left" on the registered cover by the post-man although at the material time the addressee was residing in the particular house. It was held that the tendered be fixed presumption is that the notice was duly to the addressee and the addressee must with constructive notice. Except the case reported in 52 C.W.N. 659 and AIR 1958 Cal 251, all other cases cited above were noted in that decision. The learned Single Judge of the then Dacca High Court also noticed the case of Bashir Ahmed v, Mumtaz Khan (2) where it has been held, "mere denial by the appellant that the letter or notice did not reach him or was tendered to him is not enough to rebut the presumption u/s. 27 of the General Clauses Act." 

 16. In that view of the matter the learned S.C.C. Judge acted illegally and with material irregularity in holding that the endorsement "refused" must be formally proved by the postman or by any other competent person who knew the handwriting of the postman concerned. In the instant case the plaintiff petitioner has filed ,a copy  of the notice Ext. 2, postal receipt, Ext. 3, one envelop Ext. 4 and A. D. Receipt Ext. 4(a). He has proved that he sent the notice u/s. 106 of the Transfer of Property Act by resistered post. The envelop was returned to him with the endorsement "refused." Apart from a mere denial both in his written statement and in his deposition, the opposite party has not adduced any evidence to show that he did not get an opportunity to accept notice or that he never refused it or that it was never tendered to him. As already held a mere denial is not enough to rebut the presumption of service.
